text: The fair changed this lakefront in a way that outlasted the plaster.
To carry the crowds out to Jackson Park, the city had the Illinois Central Railroad lift its tracks.
The line that ran along the lake was raised up onto a solid embankment, a long wall of earth and stone with the trains running on top.
The first ordinance for the work passed in May of 1892, a full year before the gates opened.
That wall cut the neighborhood in two.
The blocks between the tracks and the lake became a place apart, reached by ducking under the embankment, and people came to call it Hyde Park East.
The fair did not end on a high note.
Two days before it closed, a man with a grievance shot Mayor Carter Harrison dead in his own home, and the planned closing ceremony was called off.
The gates shut for good on the thirtieth of October.
The fair had done what almost no American exposition had done before.
It closed with cash left over, the first to turn a profit, even in the teeth of the depression outside.
The White City itself was already coming down, and much of what was left burned the following summer.
And the lakefront the fair had made glamorous was now valuable ground.
The question of who that ground belonged to, and who would be welcome on it, was just ahead.
